questions.question: Design a library management system. What are the key classes?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you identify core domain entities and distinguish between catalog abstraction (Book) versus physical instances (BookItem) in inventory management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers often collapse Book and BookItem into one class, missing that one book title can have multiple physical copies with independent states
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the one-to-many relationship between Book and BookItem and mention how BookItem tracks location (shelf number) and condition separately

questions.direct_answer: A library management system needs entities for catalog (Book), physical inventory (BookItem), users (Member, Librarian), and transactions (BookLending, Reservation, Fine). The key distinction is Book represents the catalog entry while BookItem represents each physical copy with its own barcode and availability status.

items: Book: catalog record (ISBN, title, authors, genre) — conceptual
BookItem: physical copy (barcode, current status, location) — physical
Member: borrower with member ID, borrow limit, current checked-out items
BookLending: transaction (who borrowed which copy when)
Reservation: member reserves a book when all copies are checked out
Fine: tracks overdue fines per member

answer_sections.content: The key design insight is separating Book (catalog concept) from BookItem (physical copy). A library has one record for 'Clean Code by Robert Martin' but 5 physical copies. When you checkout, you're checking out a BookItem, not the Book. Each BookItem has a barcode, current status (AVAILABLE, CHECKED_OUT, RESERVED), and a due date when checked out. The Member entity has a maximum borrow limit and a list of current loans. BookLending is the transaction record — created when a book is checked out, completed when returned. This models the real domain accurately: you can search for a Book, see how many copies are available, and reserve one if all are out.

follow_up_questions: How would you handle the reservation queue when a book is returned?
How do you calculate overdue fines in your design?

groups.heading: Book vs BookItem
groups.text: Book is the catalog record — ISBN, title, authors. BookItem is a physical copy — barcode, status (AVAILABLE / CHECKED_OUT / RESERVED), current due date. One Book can have many BookItems.

groups.heading: Member
groups.text: Has a member ID, a borrow limit, and a list of current loans. Can't borrow if they have outstanding fines.

groups.heading: BookLending
groups.text: The transaction record: which BookItem, which Member, checkout date, due date, return date. Created on checkout, updated on return.

groups.heading: Reservation and Fine
groups.text: Reservation holds a FIFO queue of members waiting for a book. Fine tracks overdue fees per member.

beats.text: candidates miss: the Book vs BookItem split. Without it you can't track which physical copy is where, or handle multiple copies of the same title. Always separate the catalog concept from the physical object.

speakable_v2.cap: Book is the catalog entry; BookItem is the physical copy. That one distinction unlocks the whole library design.

sections.title: Designing a Library Management System
sections.content:
The make-or-break modelling decision is separating **Book** (the catalog entry — title, author, ISBN) from **BookItem** (a single physical copy with its own barcode and status). A library owns *one* `Book` record for "Clean Code" but *five* `BookItem`s on the shelf.

From there the nouns become classes: `Member` and `Librarian` (users), `BookLending` (a checkout), `Reservation` (a hold), and `Fine` (overdue charge). The verbs — borrow, return, reserve, pay fine — become methods on the right owner.

sections.title: Approach in 5 Steps
sections.content:
| Step | Action | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Clarify | Multiple copies? Reservations? Fines? | Scope fixed |
| 2. Entities | `Book`, `BookItem`, `Member`, `Librarian`, `BookLending`, `Reservation`, `Fine` | Candidate classes |
| 3. Key split | `Book` (catalog) vs `BookItem` (physical copy) | Correct inventory model |
| 4. Relationships | `Book` 1→* `BookItem`; `Member` 1→* `BookLending` | Class diagram |
| 5. Patterns | Strategy (search, fines), Observer (reservation notify) | Extensible design |

sections.title: Java Skeleton — Book vs BookItem
Class Relationships
sections.content:
```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Book
    class BookItem
    class Member
    class Librarian
    class BookLending
    class Reservation
    class Fine
    Book "1" *-- "*" BookItem : copies
    Member "1" --> "*" BookLending : borrows
    BookItem --> BookLending
    Book "1" --> "*" Reservation : queue
    Member --> Fine : owes
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Merging Book and BookItem** — then you can't track which physical copy is out, or have 5 copies of one title.
- **Borrowing a `Book`** — you borrow a `BookItem`; the catalog entry isn't checkout-able.
- **A God `Library` class** doing search, lending, and fines — split by responsibility (SRP).
- **No member borrowing rules** — `canBorrow()` should gate on outstanding fines and loan count.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Book = catalog**, **BookItem = physical copy** — the central distinction.
- `Book` 1→* `BookItem`; `Member` 1→* `BookLending`.
- Borrow/return operate on `BookItem`; status enum tracks availability.
- **Strategy** for search & fines, **Observer** for reservation notifications.
- `Member.canBorrow()` enforces fine/loan-limit invariants.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I'd lead with the single most important modelling decision, because it's where most people slip: separating Book from BookItem. A Book is the catalog entry — title, author, ISBN — and there's exactly one per title. A BookItem is a single physical copy with its own barcode and an availability status. So the library has one Book record for Clean Code but maybe five BookItems on the shelf. A member borrows a BookItem, never the abstract Book, because you can only physically check out a copy.

From there the other classes follow naturally. Member and Librarian are the users, with Librarian having extra permissions. BookLending represents an active checkout, capturing the item, the member, the issue date, and the due date. Reservation is a hold on a title, and Fine is an overdue charge. The relationships are a Book having many BookItems by composition, and a Member having many active loans.

I'd put borrowing rules on the Member — a canBorrow method that checks they have no outstanding fines and haven't hit the loan limit. For behaviour, I'd mention I'd use Strategy for search and fine calculation so those can vary, and Observer so that when a copy is returned, the next member in the reservation queue gets notified. The big mistake to avoid is collapsing Book and BookItem into one class, because then you simply can't represent multiple copies or know which one is checked out.

questions.question: How do you handle the book reservation system in LLD?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you model ordered waitlists and implement the Observer pattern to handle asynchronous notification when inventory becomes available
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers often use a simple list without FIFO ordering or forget to notify waiting members when a book returns, breaking the reservation flow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention expiration timers—if the notified member doesn't pick up the book within 24 hours, move to the next reservation in queue

questions.direct_answer: Use a queue per Book to store Reservations in order. When a Member reserves, append to the queue. On BookItem return, the Book checks its reservation queue and notifies the first Member. Implement Observer pattern where BookItem notifies Book of status changes, and Book processes the next pending Reservation.

answer_sections.content: When all copies of a book are checked out, members can join a reservation queue. The queue is on the Book entity. When a BookItem is returned, it notifies the Book. Book checks if there's a reservation — if yes, it processes the reservation: assigns the returned BookItem to the first member in queue and sends them a notification. Observer pattern works naturally here: BookItem is the observable, Book (or ReservationManager) is the observer. The notification to the member (email/SMS) can be an event published to a notification service — keeping the library domain clean and not mixing notification infrastructure into domain classes.

follow_up_questions: How long should a reservation be held before expiring?
What data structure is best for the reservation queue and why?

beats.text: When all copies of a book are checked out, members join a reservation queue. The queue lives on the Book entity. When any BookItem is returned, the queue is processed.

items: Book holds a Queue of Reservation objects — FIFO ensures fairness
When a member reserves, add a new Reservation to the queue
When a BookItem is returned, notify the Book via Observer
Book polls the queue: if someone's waiting, assign the returned BookItem to them
Send the member a notification — but keep notification logic out of the domain class

beats.text: Observer pattern: BookItem is the observable. On return, it calls onBookItemReturned() on the Book. Book processes the head of its reservation queue and fires a ReservationAvailableEvent for the notification service to handle.
non-obvious: keep email and SMS notification logic out of the Book class. Publish an event and let a separate notification service consume it. This keeps your domain model clean and testable.

speakable_v2.cap: Queue on Book for FIFO fairness. Observer to trigger it on return. Fire an event for notifications — don't put email logic in your domain class.

sections.title: The Book Reservation System
sections.content:
Reservations are about **fairness**: whoever reserved first should get the next available copy. So each `Book` keeps a **FIFO queue** of `Reservation`s. When a member reserves an unavailable title, you append them. When a `BookItem` is **returned**, the `Book` pops the head of the queue and **notifies** that member.

The clean way to wire the notification is the **Observer pattern**: the `BookItem` tells the `Book` its status changed, and the `Book` processes the next reservation — no tight coupling between return logic and notification.

sections.title: Java — FIFO Reservation Queue + Notify
Reservation Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Member reserves
(title unavailable)"] --> B["Append to FIFO queue"] C["Copy returned"] --> D{"Queue empty?"} D -- "No" --> E["Pop head,
hold copy, notify member"] D -- "Yes" --> F["Mark copy AVAILABLE"] ```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using a Set or list without order** — breaks first-come-first-served fairness; use a `Queue`.
- **Coupling return logic to notifications** — a returned book directly emailing users. Use Observer so the `Book` decides.
- **No hold/expiry** — the reserved copy should be held only for a window, then offered to the next member.
- **Reserving at `BookItem` level** — reservations are per *title* (`Book`), satisfied by any copy.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- One **FIFO `Queue` of `Reservation`s per `Book`** = fairness.
- On return, **pop the head** and notify that member; else mark available.
- **Observer**: `BookItem` notifies `Book`; `Book` processes the queue.
- Reservations are per **title**, satisfied by **any copy**.
- Add a **hold window** so a held copy doesn't block forever.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I'd treat reservations as a fairness problem: the member who reserved first should get the next copy. So each Book keeps a FIFO queue of reservations. When a member wants a title that's currently all checked out, I append a Reservation to that book's queue with a timestamp. The queue ordering is what guarantees first-come-first-served.

The interesting part is what happens on return. When any physical copy of that title comes back, the system needs to check the reservation queue and, if someone's waiting, hold the copy for them and notify them rather than just putting it back on the shelf. I'd wire this with the Observer pattern: the BookItem notifies its Book that its status changed, and the Book handles the logic — it polls the head of the queue, and if there's a member waiting, it marks the copy reserved and sends them a notification through a NotificationService. If the queue is empty, it just marks the copy available. The Observer indirection keeps the return logic decoupled from the notification mechanism, so I can swap email for SMS without touching the return flow.

A couple of refinements I'd mention: reservations should be at the title level, not a specific copy, because any returned copy satisfies the hold. And I'd add a hold window — the reserved copy is kept for the member for, say, 48 hours, after which it rolls to the next person, so a no-show doesn't block everyone behind them.

questions.question: How do you model search functionality in the library system?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you apply the Strategy pattern to decouple search implementation from the catalog interface, demonstrating knowledge of behavioral design patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers hardcode multiple search methods in LibraryCatalog (searchByTitle, searchByAuthor) creating a bloated class that violates Open-Closed Principle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention combining criteria with Composite pattern for advanced searches like author AND genre or suggest indexing strategies for performance

questions.direct_answer: Use the Strategy pattern with a SearchCriteria interface. Implementations like SearchByTitle, SearchByAuthor, SearchByISBN, SearchByGenre encapsulate different search algorithms. LibraryCatalog accepts any SearchCriteria and delegates to its execute method. This keeps search logic decoupled and makes adding new criteria trivial.

answer_sections.content: For search, I use the Strategy pattern. SearchCriteria is an interface with one method: matches(Book). Each search type is a separate implementation: TitleSearchCriteria, AuthorSearchCriteria, ISBNCriteria, GenreCriteria. The catalog's search method takes any SearchCriteria — it doesn't know or care which one. This makes the design open for extension: adding a SearchByPublicationYear requires a new class, no changes to catalog. You can also compose criteria: new AndCriteria(new TitleCriteria('Java'), new AuthorCriteria('Bloch')) for multi-field search. This is the Specification pattern used in DDD, and it maps cleanly to database queries if you extend it.

follow_up_questions: How would you add full-text search to the library catalog?
What is the Specification pattern and how does it relate to this design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a library management system
speakable_v2.hook: Search by title, author, ISBN, genre — that's four algorithms behind one operation, which is the textbook cue for Strategy.

beats.text: Library search uses the Strategy pattern. SearchCriteria is an interface with a single matches(Book) method. Each search type is a separate implementation. The catalog's search method accepts any SearchCriteria.

items: SearchCriteria interface: boolean matches(Book book)
TitleSearchCriteria: checks if title contains the query (case-insensitive)
AuthorSearchCriteria: checks if any author name matches
ISBNSearchCriteria: exact match on ISBN
AndCriteria: composes two criteria — both must match

beats.text: To search for a Java book by Joshua Bloch: new AndCriteria(new TitleCriteria('Java'), new AuthorCriteria('Bloch')). Adding a new search type — like SearchByPublicationYear — is a new class, not a change to LibraryCatalog.
non-obvious: this pattern is called the Specification pattern in Domain-Driven Design. If an interviewer asks about Specification, this is the answer — it's Strategy applied to filtering predicates.

speakable_v2.cap: SearchCriteria interface + one class per search type + composable with AndCriteria. Open for extension, zero changes to the catalog.
followup_handoff: How would you add full-text search?

sections.title: Modelling Search Functionality
sections.content:
Members search by **title, author, ISBN, or genre** — same operation, different algorithm each time. That's the cue for the **Strategy pattern**: a `SearchStrategy` interface with one `search` method, and an implementation per criterion (`SearchByTitle`, `SearchByAuthor`, ...).

The `LibraryCatalog` accepts any `SearchStrategy` and delegates. Adding *search by publication year* later is a new class — the catalog never changes. For real performance you'd also keep **indexes** (a `Map<String, List<Book>>` by author, etc.) so search isn't a full scan.

sections.title: Without Strategy — one method that keeps growing
With Strategy — one class per criterion
Search Strategy Structure
sections.content:
```mermaid
classDiagram
    class SearchStrategy {
        <<interface>>
        +search(catalog, term) List~Book~
    }
    class SearchByTitle
    class SearchByAuthor
    class SearchByISBN
    class LibraryCatalog
    SearchStrategy <|.. SearchByTitle
    SearchStrategy <|.. SearchByAuthor
    SearchStrategy <|.. SearchByISBN
    LibraryCatalog --> SearchStrategy : delegates
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **A growing if-else on search type** — exactly what Strategy removes.
- **Full linear scan every time** — fine to mention, but add indexes (`Map` by author/genre) for scale.
- **Search logic inside `Book`** — `Book` is data; searching is the catalog's/strategy's job.
- **Case-sensitive matching** — use `equalsIgnoreCase`/`contains` so users find results.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- One operation, many algorithms → **Strategy pattern**.
- `SearchStrategy` interface; one class per criterion (title/author/ISBN/genre).
- `LibraryCatalog` **delegates**; new criterion = new class (Open/Closed).
- Back it with **indexes** (`Map`) to avoid full scans at scale.
- Keep matching **case-insensitive** for usability.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Searching by title, author, ISBN, or genre is the same operation with a different algorithm behind it each time, and that's the classic signal for the Strategy pattern. I'd define a SearchStrategy interface with a single search method that takes the catalog and a search term and returns matching books. Then each criterion is its own class — SearchByTitle, SearchByAuthor, SearchByISBN, SearchByGenre — each implementing that method with its own filtering logic.

The LibraryCatalog holds the books and exposes a search method that takes a SearchStrategy and delegates to it. So the catalog never needs to know how a particular search works; it just passes the call through. The big win is extensibility: when someone asks to add search by publication year, that's a brand new class implementing the interface, and I don't touch the catalog at all. That's the Open/Closed Principle.

Compare that to the naive approach, which is one search method with a long if-else or switch on a type string. Every new criterion means editing and retesting that one method, and it grows without bound.

For a real system I'd add one more point: a pure Strategy still scans the whole catalog, which is fine for an interview but slow at scale. So I'd back it with indexes — maps keyed by author or genre — so the strategy can look up rather than scan. And I'd keep the matching case-insensitive so users actually find what they're after.

questions.question: How do you handle fines in the library management system?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you handle temporal calculations and state management for financial transactions, showing understanding of date arithmetic and business rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers often calculate fine as a simple subtraction without handling edge cases like partial days, weekends, or grace periods, or fail to block borrowing for outstanding fines
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention grace period (first day free), weekend/holiday exclusion from fine calculation, or progressive fine rates (higher after 30 days overdue)

questions.direct_answer: Calculate fine during book return by comparing return date to due date. If overdue, fine equals overdue days multiplied by daily rate. Use a FineCalculator strategy to encapsulate rate logic (standard, premium members might have different rates). Member entity tracks outstanding fine balance that must be cleared before new borrowing is allowed.

answer_sections.content: Fine calculation is straightforward: when a book is returned, compare the return date to the due date on the BookLending record. If return date > due date, calculate overdueDays and multiply by the daily rate. I use a FineCalculator Strategy so the rate and calculation method can change without modifying the checkout process. The Member entity has an outstandingFines balance. A business rule: members with outstanding fines can't borrow new books until they pay. The FinePayment creates a transaction record and reduces the balance. Like fee calculation in parking lots, I use BigDecimal for money — double arithmetic has floating-point precision issues that would make accounting incorrect.

follow_up_questions: What if a member disputes a fine — how would you handle that in the design?
Should fines be calculated lazily (on return) or eagerly (each day)?

speakable_v2.hook: Fines look like simple arithmetic until you realise the rate itself is a policy that changes per member tier — Strategy again.

beats.text: When a book is returned, compare the return date to the due date on the BookLending record. If it's overdue, calculate the fine as overdue days times the daily rate.

items: FineCalculator interface: calculate(BookLending, returnDate) returns BigDecimal
StandardFineCalculator: DAILY_RATE times max(0, overdueDays) — zero if returned on time
Member entity tracks outstandingFines balance
Business rule: members with outstanding fines can't borrow new books

beats.text: FineCalculator is a Strategy: StandardFineCalculator, WeekdayOnlyFineCalculator, or GracePeriodFineCalculator can all plug in without changing the checkout process.

production trap: use BigDecimal for fine amounts — never double. Floating-point rounding errors compound in financial calculations and would make accounting incorrect. This is true for any money calculation in Java.

speakable_v2.cap: FineCalculator as a Strategy, BigDecimal for amounts, outstanding balance on Member with a borrow-block rule. Simple design, production-ready thinking.
followup_handoff: How would you handle fine disputes in the design?
Should fines be calculated lazily on return or eagerly each day?

sections.title: Handling Fines
sections.content:
A fine is computed on **return**: compare the return date to the due date, and if overdue, charge **overdue days × daily rate**. The subtlety is that the *rate* is a **policy** — standard members, premium members, and students may differ — so wrap it in a `FineStrategy` (Strategy pattern again).

The `Member` tracks an **outstanding fine balance** that must be cleared before borrowing again — an invariant enforced by `canBorrow()`. Use `BigDecimal` for the money.

sections.title: Java — Fine Calculation on Return
Fine Flow on Return
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Return book"] --> B{"returnDate > dueDate?"} B -- "No" --> C["No fine,
mark available"] B -- "Yes" --> D["fine = days * rate"] D --> E["Add to member's
outstanding balance"] ```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Hard-coding one rate** — different tiers need different rates; use a `FineStrategy`.
- **`double` for money** — rounding errors. Use `BigDecimal`.
- **Computing fines on a schedule** — compute on return (or on demand), not via a nightly job for the interview scope.
- **Letting members borrow with unpaid fines** — `canBorrow()` must check the outstanding balance.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Fine = **overdue days × daily rate**, computed on return.
- Rate is a **policy** → `FineStrategy` per member tier.
- `Member` tracks an **outstanding balance**; `canBorrow()` enforces clearing it.
- Use **`BigDecimal`**, never `double`, for money.
- Use `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between` for clean date math.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Fines are calculated when a book is returned. I compare the return date with the due date, and if the book is overdue, the fine is the number of overdue days times a daily rate. I'd compute the days with ChronoUnit.DAYS.between, and I'd use BigDecimal for the money, never double, because floating point rounding causes real problems with currency.

The part that makes this more than arithmetic is that the rate isn't fixed — it's a policy. A standard member, a premium member, and a student might all have different daily rates, and the library might run a fine-free week. So I'd wrap the rate in a FineStrategy interface with implementations like StandardFine and PremiumFine. The return service takes whichever strategy applies to that member and asks it for the rate. Adding a new tier is then a new strategy class, not a change to the return logic.

The other half is the member side. The Member entity tracks an outstanding fine balance. When a fine is incurred, it's added to that balance, and crucially the member's canBorrow method checks that the balance is clear before allowing new loans. That makes 'you can't borrow until you've paid your fines' an invariant the design enforces, rather than a rule someone has to remember to apply. For the interview scope I'd compute fines on return or on demand rather than building a nightly batch job, and mention the batch approach only if asked about scale.

questions.question: What are the key design decisions in the library management system?

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you articulate design rationale and justify architectural choices, showing understanding of trade-offs and pattern selection criteria
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers list design patterns without explaining why they were chosen or fail to connect decisions to real library operations and scalability needs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explicitly mention trade-offs for each decision and alternative approaches you considered, showing depth of analysis beyond pattern matching

questions.direct_answer: Key decisions: separate Book (catalog) from BookItem (physical copy) for inventory tracking, use Queue for FIFO reservation fairness, apply Strategy pattern for extensible search and fine calculation, implement Observer pattern for return notifications, and define role-based permissions with Member versus Librarian classes for access control.

answer_sections.content: The design decisions I'm most deliberate about: Book vs BookItem — the hardest part for beginners is realizing a library book has two representations. Without this separation, you can't track which physical copy is where or handle multiple copies. Reservation queue as a Queue (FIFO) — because reservation fairness matters: first come, first served. Strategy for FineCalculator — libraries change their fine policies, so this needs to be swappable. Observer for notifications — when a book is available, the right member needs to know; Observer decouples the availability tracking from notification logic. Role separation between Member and Librarian: Librarian can add books, block members, adjust fines; Member can search and borrow. These could be separate classes or role-based permissions.

follow_up_questions: How would you add digital/e-book support to this design?
What would change if the library allowed inter-library loans?

beats.text: Each key design decision in a library system has a specific reason. Being able to state those reasons is what separates a strong LLD candidate from someone who just lists classes.

groups.heading: Book vs BookItem
groups.text: Without this split you can't track multiple physical copies or show per-copy availability. It's the most important distinction in this design.

groups.heading: Queue for reservations
groups.text: FIFO ensures fairness — first reserved, first served. A List would work but Queue communicates the intent clearly.

groups.heading: Strategy for fines and search
groups.text: Both change independently of the checkout flow. Strategy lets you add new policies or search types without modifying existing classes.

groups.heading: Observer for return notifications
groups.text: Decouples availability tracking from notification delivery. The domain class shouldn't know about email or SMS.

groups.heading: Member vs Librarian roles
groups.text: Different permissions: Librarian adds books, blocks members, adjusts fines. Member searches and borrows. Separate classes or role-based access — either is defensible.

beats.text: non-obvious: interviewers often ask 'why did you use a Queue here instead of a List?' Be ready — the answer is FIFO semantics and intent clarity, not just performance.

speakable_v2.cap: For every class and pattern you introduce, be ready to say the one sentence that justifies it. That fluency is the mark of a strong LLD candidate.

What would change for inter-library loans?

sections.title: Key Design Decisions
sections.content:
When asked to summarise, replay your design as **deliberate decisions with reasons** — that's what signals seniority. The five that matter here:

- **Book vs BookItem** — catalog entry vs physical copy, so you can track multiple copies and which one is out.
- **FIFO `Queue` for reservations** — fairness, first-come-first-served.
- **Strategy** for search and fines — extensible without editing core code.
- **Observer** for return notifications — decoupled.
- **Role-based access** — `Member` vs `Librarian` for permissions.

sections.title: Java — Role-Based Permissions
Decisions at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Book vs BookItem|~Catalog vs copy|track many copies|know which is out|core inventory split
emerald|FIFO Reservations|~Fairness|Queue per title|first-come served|hold window
violet|Strategy|~Search & fines|interface + impls|Open/Closed|new rule = new class
amber|Observer|~Return notify|decoupled|copy notifies title|swap email/SMS freely
rose|Role access|~Member vs Librarian|inheritance|permission methods|least privilege

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Summarising structure only** — also state *why* each decision was made.
- **No access control** — a `Member` shouldn't delete catalog entries; model roles.
- **Forgetting trade-offs** — e.g. denormalizing availability counts for fast display vs consistency cost.
- **Over-patterning** — only highlight patterns that solved a real problem in your design.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Book vs BookItem** split = correct multi-copy inventory.
- **FIFO `Queue`** = fair reservations.
- **Strategy** (search, fines) + **Observer** (notifications) = extensible, decoupled.
- **Role-based access**: `Member` vs `Librarian` via inheritance.
- Present decisions **with reasons and trade-offs**, not just a class list.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I'd close by replaying the design as a set of deliberate decisions, each with the reasoning, because that's far more convincing than re-listing classes. The first and most important decision was separating Book from BookItem — the catalog entry from the physical copy — which is what lets the library hold multiple copies of a title and know exactly which one is checked out.

The second decision was using a FIFO queue per title for reservations, because reservations are fundamentally a fairness problem and a queue guarantees first-come-first-served. Third, I used the Strategy pattern for both search and fine calculation, because those are the parts most likely to change — new search criteria, new fine rates per member tier — and Strategy lets me add them as new classes without touching existing code. Fourth, I used the Observer pattern for return notifications, so that when a copy comes back the next reserver is notified without coupling the return logic to the notification channel. Fifth, I modelled role-based access with a User base class and Member and Librarian subclasses, so privileged actions like managing the catalog or waiving fines are gated by permission methods.

I'd also volunteer a trade-off or two — for instance, denormalizing an availability count onto Book for fast display, at the cost of keeping it in sync. Naming the decisions, the reasons, and the trade-offs is what makes the summary land as senior-level rather than a recap.
